p: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.

notes: The article spells the successor both Panduvasudeva and Panduvasdeva; I used the first.
The article gives the dates as 'c. 543-505 BCE' and calls him 'a legendary king'; everything here is the chronicles' account and is worded so.
The existing description says he 'founded the settlement of Tambapanni'; the article says he landed in the area known as Tambapanni and that the kingdom was so named.
